subject: Chemistry
title: The Thermite Reaction
description: A quick, practical guide to The Thermite Reaction.

hook.text: Mix iron oxide and aluminum powder, light it, and it burns at 2,500°C—hot enough to melt through steel.

buildup.text: Thermite is an exothermic reaction where aluminum steals oxygen from iron oxide at extreme speed.

discovery.text: The reaction produces molten iron and aluminum oxide. It's so hot it can weld railroad tracks on site.

twist.text: Once started, thermite can't be stopped. Water makes it worse—steam explosions scatter molten metal.

climax.text: Railroad companies still use thermite welding today. Two powders create a forge anywhere.

punchline.text: Rust plus aluminum powder. Instant forge at 2,500°C.

quiz.question: Why can't you extinguish a thermite reaction with water?
options: The extreme heat causes steam explosions that scatter molten metal
Water is a fuel for thermite reactions
Thermite absorbs water and grows larger

details.summary: The thermite reaction combines aluminum powder with iron oxide to produce molten iron and aluminum oxide at temperatures exceeding 2,500 degrees Celsius. This intensely exothermic reaction is used for welding railroad tracks, cutting through metal, and in military applications.
details.whyItMatters: Thermite demonstrates how enormous energy can be stored in seemingly stable powders. Its practical applications range from railroad maintenance to emergency metal cutting in industrial settings.
takeaways: Thermite reaches temperatures above 2,500 degrees Celsius
The reaction produces molten iron from powdered ingredients
Railroad thermite welding creates seamless track joints

faq.question: Why is the thermite reaction so difficult to ignite accidentally?
faq.answer: Thermite requires an ignition temperature of about 1,500 degrees Celsius, far above what a match or lighter can provide. A magnesium ribbon or sparkler is typically needed to start the reaction, making accidental ignition rare.

faq.question: Can water extinguish a thermite reaction once it starts?
faq.answer: No. Water actually makes thermite more dangerous because the extreme heat instantly decomposes water into hydrogen and oxygen, which can cause a steam explosion. Sand or dry chemical agents are the only safe suppression methods.
